analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from counting the cost of carbon pollution in rulemaking.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred federal agencies from counting the cost of carbon pollution when weighing rules, never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit the Energy Department, EPA, Interior Department, Transportation Department, and the Council on Environmental Quality from using the government's estimates of the cost of carbon, methane, and nitrous oxide pollution when they write or justify rules — unless a new law authorizes it or the estimate meets strict budget-office rules: only domestic (not worldwide) damages and high discount rates that shrink future costs [S2][S3]. Those cost estimates are what make climate and pollution rules pencil out; without them, the benefits of cutting emissions count for little on paper [S3]. The bill also required EPA to report how often agencies had used these cost estimates since 2009 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters. The bill's own text singles out EPA methane rules for the oil and gas sector, power-plant carbon rules, and an Interior rule on methane waste from drilling as actions justified by these cost estimates [S3]. By barring or narrowing the cost side of the ledger, the bill would make such rules far harder to defend, reducing compliance costs for oil, gas, and coal producers. The public would continue to bear the damages from emissions — health costs, extreme weather, and a warmer climate — that the estimates are designed to measure [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would bar five agencies from considering the social cost of carbon, methane, nitrous oxide, or any greenhouse gas in any rulemaking, guidance, or agency action, unless a new federal law explicitly authorizes it or the estimate complies with OMB Circular A-4 [S2][S3].

The permitted alternative would count only domestic costs and benefits and use the 3- and 7-percent discount rates in Circular A-4, which produces much lower damage estimates than the existing interagency figures [S2][S3].
It would require EPA to report, within 120 days of enactment, how many rules, guidance documents, and agency actions since January 2009 used these social cost estimates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs of greenhouse gas emissions would go uncounted (or counted at a steep discount) in federal decisions, so the public — through health impacts, climate damages, and environmental degradation — would absorb harms that no longer appear on the regulatory balance sheet [S3]. Communities affected by oil and gas methane pollution and by power-plant emissions would lose a key justification for protective rules, which the bill's findings identify specifically [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public bearing pollution and climate harms

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings argue the existing estimates were developed by an interagency working group without public notice-and-comment or rigorous peer review, and that they used global damages and discount rates outside OMB's Circular A-4 guidance — a good-faith process objection [S3].

Counting only domestic damages and using high discount rates sharply lowers the measured cost of each ton of carbon, because most climate harm falls outside U.S. borders and the worst effects fall on future generations [S3]. Under that accounting, climate rules would usually fail their own cost-benefit test and be much harder to adopt or defend in court.

The restrictions would apply not only to cost-benefit analyses but to any rulemaking, guidance, or agency action, and would block the existing estimates even as justification — a sweeping constraint on how agencies weigh climate harm [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose a real methodological constraint on how agencies weigh climate damages, which supporters frame as a transparency and process fix. But the practical effect runs one way: it would strip or shrink the benefit side of the ledger for pollution rules while leaving the compliance costs fully counted, tilting the scale against rules that protect air quality and public health. The cost of that tilt falls on the public; the savings fall on fossil fuel producers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. James Lankford introduced S. 1512 on June 29, 2017, with five original cosponsors: Sens. Cornyn, Inhofe, Barrasso, and Blunt [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction; that referral was the only action it ever received [S5].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people exposed to pollution and climate damages came out ahead on this bill: it died without a vote, so the statutory accounting tool for valuing carbon and methane harm was not dismantled. Fossil fuel producers gained ground on the policy through the executive actions the bill builds on (Executive Orders 13777 and 13783, cited in the bill itself), but not through this legislation [S3].

for.name: James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar agencies from using the social cost of carbon and related estimates [S1][S3].

for.name: 7 of 52 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or Independent did [S4].

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: John Barrasso, R-WY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from June 2017 until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters (the sponsor and seven cosponsors) were Republicans, including the chairman of the committee of referral; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill's findings target EPA oil and gas methane standards as rules justified by the social cost of methane [S3]. Barring or shrinking that cost estimate would make methane rules harder to justify, cutting compliance costs for producers while leaving the public to bear the pollution.
The findings describe the cost estimates as a tool to justify regulating or prohibiting the use of coal and other fossil fuels [S3]. Removing that tool would ease regulatory pressure on coal.

Power-plant carbon rules were justified using the social cost of carbon [S3]; the bill would weaken the case for such standards, lowering compliance costs for carbon-intensive generators while shifting pollution and climate costs to the public.
